comments.text:
Hey Dr. Mike, I just want to thank you for everything you’ve taught about first aid and what to do until an ambulance arrives.
Early this morning, on my way to work, a man collapsed in the metro — it looked like a cardiac arrest. A police officer, a metro worker, a passerby, and I were the ones who responded. I was the only one who remembered how to do CPR (I took my mandatory first aid course about 8 months ago for my driver’s license, per EU rules).
Once I started CPR, your advice immediately came back to me. I assigned roles by asking who else knew CPR so we could rotate. I instructed the passerby how to hold the man’s head to keep the airway open, and the police officer had already radioed for an ambulance.
When I got tired, I told another person to switch with me and emphasized deep, fast compressions at a manageable pace. I also reassured him with what you always say: “Good CPR breaks ribs,” so not to worry and to keep going.
When others started wondering if the man was already dead, I kept insisting that we must not stop and that only the medical team can make that decision.
We performed CPR continuously for almost 15 minutes. By the end I was completely exhausted, barely able to continue, and the police officer stepped in as well (before that he was managing the situation and keeping the area clear so other trains could continue running).
The ambulance was unfortunately very late — not due to the crew, but because emergency services here are severely understaffed, which is a well-known issue in the city.
When the ambulance finally arrived, the team was initially about to pronounce him dead. But when we told them that he had occasional breathing-like gasps during CPR and that compressions had never stopped, they immediately loaded him and continued treatment.
I honestly don’t know if he survived, or how long he had been unresponsive before we got to him. But I do know that your teachings helped me stay calm, give clear instructions, and make the best possible use of the people around me.
Thank you for that, I just wanted to say that what you teach reach far and helps a lot of people even someone across the ocean like me.

comments.text: What I've gathered regarding the being cold vs catching a cold thing is that being cold doesn't CAUSE you to get sick, but prolonged exposure to low temperatures is a risk factor that increases your chances of getting sick. Ultimately, you need to have been exposed to a cold virus to catch a cold, but being exposed to a virus + low temperatures makes you more likely to get sick, and makes you get MORE sick than you otherwise would have done.
